{{Short description|Set theory concept}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[set theory]], a '''measurable cardinal''' is a certain kind of [[large cardinal]] number. In order to define the concept, one introduces a two-valued [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] on a cardinal <math>\kappa</math>, or more generally on any set. For a cardinal <math>\kappa</math>, it can be described as a subdivision of all of its [[subset]]s into large and small sets such that <math>\kappa</math> itself is large, the [[empty set]] and all [[singleton (mathematics)|singleton]]s <math>\{\alpha\}</math> with <math>\alpha\in\kappa</math> are small, [[set complement|complement]]s of small sets are large and vice versa. The [[intersection]] of fewer than <math>\kappa</math> large sets is again large.<ref>{{harvnb|Maddy|1988}}</ref>

It turns out that [[uncountable]] cardinals endowed with a two-valued measure are large cardinals whose existence cannot be proved from [[ZFC]].<ref>{{harvnb|Jech|2002}}</ref>

The concept of a measurable cardinal was introduced by [[Stanisław Ulam]] in 1930.<ref>{{harvnb|Ulam|1930}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Formally, a measurable cardinal is an uncountable [[cardinal number]] <math>\kappa</math> such that there exists a <math>\kappa</math>-additive, non-trivial, 0-1-valued [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] <math>\mu</math> on the [[power set]] of <math>\kappa</math>.

Here, <math>\kappa</math>-additive means that for every <math>\lambda<\kappa</math> and every <math>\lambda</math>-sized collection <math>\{A_\beta\}_{\beta<\lambda}</math> of pairwise disjoint subsets <math>A_\beta\subseteq\kappa</math>, we have
:<math>\mu\Big(\bigcup_{\beta<\lambda}A_\beta\Big)=\sum_{\beta<\lambda}\mu(A_\beta)</math>.

Equivalently, <math>\kappa</math> is a measurable cardinal if and only if it is an uncountable cardinal with a <math>\kappa</math>-complete, non-principal [[ultrafilter]]. This means that the intersection of any ''strictly less than'' <math>\kappa</math>-many sets in the ultrafilter is also in the ultrafilter.

Equivalently, <math>\kappa</math> is measurable if it is the [[critical point (set theory)|critical point]] of a non-trivial [[elementary embedding]] of the [[universe (set theory)|universe]] <math>V</math> into a [[transitive class]] <math>M</math> and <math>^\kappa M\subseteq M</math>. This equivalence is due to [[Jerome Keisler]] and [[Dana Scott]], and uses the [[ultraproduct|ultrapower]] construction from [[model theory]]. Since <math>V</math> is a [[proper class]], a technical problem that is not usually present when considering ultrapowers needs to be addressed, by what is now called [[Scott's trick]].

== Properties ==
It is trivial to note that if <math>\kappa</math> admits a non-trivial <math>\kappa</math>-additive measure, then <math>\kappa</math> must be [[regular cardinal|regular]]: by non-triviality and <math>\kappa</math>-additivity, any subset of cardinality less than <math>\kappa</math> must have measure 0, and then by <math>\kappa</math>-additivity again, this means that the entire set must not be a union of fewer than <math>\kappa</math> sets of cardinality less than <math>\kappa</math>. Finally, if <math>\lambda<\kappa</math> then it can't be the case that <math>\kappa\leq 2^\lambda</math>. If this were the case, we could identify <math>\kappa</math> with some collection of 0-1 sequences of length <math>\lambda</math>. For each position in the sequence, either the subset of sequences with 1 in that position or the subset with 0 in that position would have to have measure 1. The intersection of these <math>\lambda</math>-many measure 1 subsets would thus also have to have measure 1, but it would contain exactly one sequence, which would contradict the non-triviality of the measure. Thus, assuming the [[axiom of choice]] (as the trichotomy of cardinality between &kappa; and 2<sup>&lambda;</sup>), we can infer that <math>\kappa</math> is a [[strong limit cardinal]], which completes the proof of its [[inaccessible cardinal|inaccessibility]].

Although it follows from [[ZFC]] that every measurable cardinal is [[inaccessible cardinal|inaccessible]] (and is [[Ineffable cardinal|ineffable]], [[Ramsey cardinal|Ramsey]], etc.), it is consistent with [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|ZF]] that a measurable cardinal can be a [[successor cardinal]]. It follows from ZF&nbsp;+&nbsp;[[axiom of determinacy|AD]] that <math>\omega_1</math> is measurable,<ref name="JechDeterminacy81">T. Jech, "[https://projecteuclid.org/journalArticle/Download?urlid=bams%2F1183548432 The Brave New World of Determinacy]" (PDF download). Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, vol. 5, number 3, November 1981 (pp.339--349).</ref> and that every subset of <math>\omega_1</math> contains or is disjoint from a [[club set|closed and unbounded]] subset.

Ulam showed that the smallest cardinal <math>\kappa</math> that admits a non-trivial countably-additive two-valued measure must in fact admit a <math>\kappa</math>-additive measure. (If there were some collection of fewer than <math>\kappa</math> measure-0 subsets whose union was <math>\kappa</math>, then the induced measure on this collection would be a counterexample to the minimality of <math>\kappa</math>.) From there, one can prove (with the axiom of choice) that the least such cardinal must be inaccessible.

If <math>\kappa</math> is measurable and <math>p\in V_\kappa</math> and <math>M</math> (the ultrapower of <math>V</math>) satisfies <math>\psi(\kappa,p)</math>, then the set of <math>\alpha<\kappa</math> such that <math>V</math> satisfies <math>\psi(\alpha,p)</math> is stationary in <math>\kappa</math> (actually a set of measure 1). In particular, if <math>\psi</math> is a <math>\Pi_1</math> formula and <math>V</math> satisfies <math>\psi(\kappa,p)</math>, then <math>M</math> satisfies it and thus <math>V</math> satisfies <math>\psi(\alpha,p)</math> for a stationary set of <math>\alpha<\kappa</math>. This property can be used to show that <math>\kappa</math> is a limit of most types of large cardinals that are weaker than measurable. Notice that the ultrafilter or measure witnessing that <math>\kappa</math> is measurable cannot be in <math>M</math> since the smallest such measurable cardinal would have to have another such below it, which is impossible.

If one starts with an elementary embedding <math>j_1</math> of <math>V</math> into <math>M_1</math> with [[critical point (set theory)|critical point]] <math>\kappa</math>, then one can define an ultrafilter <math>U</math> on <math>\kappa</math> as <math>\{S\subseteq\kappa \mid \kappa\in j_1(S)\}</math>. Then, taking an ultrapower of <math>V</math> over <math>U</math>, we can get another elementary embedding <math>j_2</math> of <math>V</math> into <math>M_2</math>. However, it is important to remember that <math>j_2\neq j_1</math>. Thus, other types of large cardinals such as [[strong cardinal]]s may also be measurable, but not using the same embedding. It can be shown that a strong cardinal <math>\kappa</math> is measurable and also has <math>\kappa</math>-many measurable cardinals below it.

Every measurable cardinal <math>\kappa</math> is a 0-[[huge cardinal]] because <math>^\kappa M\subseteq M</math>, that is, every function from <math>\kappa</math> to <math>M</math>, is in <math>M</math>. Consequently, <math>V_{\kappa+1}\subseteq M</math>.

==Implications of existence==
If a measurable cardinal exists, every set of reals at level <math>\mathbf{\Sigma}^1_2</math> of the [[projective hierarchy]] is [[Lebesgue-measurable set|Lebesgue-measurable]].

== Real-valued measurable ==
A cardinal <math>\kappa</math> is called '''real-valued measurable''' if there is a <math>\kappa</math>-additive [[probability measure]] on the power set of <math>\kappa</math> that vanishes on singletons. Real-valued measurable cardinals were introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Stefan Banach|first=Stefan|last=Banach|year=1930}}. {{harvtxt|Banach|Kuratowski|1929}} showed that  the [[continuum hypothesis]] implies that <math>\mathfrak{c}</math> is not real-valued measurable. {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Stanislaw Ulam|first=Stanislaw|last= Ulam|year=1930}} showed (see below for parts of Ulam's proof) that real valued measurable cardinals are weakly inaccessible (they are in fact [[weakly Mahlo]]).  All measurable cardinals are real-valued measurable, and a real-valued measurable cardinal <math>\kappa</math> is measurable if and only if <math>\kappa</math> is greater than <math>\mathfrak{c}</math>. Thus a cardinal is measurable if and only if it is real-valued measurable and strongly inaccessible. A real valued measurable cardinal less than or equal to <math>\mathfrak{c}</math> exists if and only if there is a [[sigma additivity|countably additive]] extension of the [[Lebesgue measure]] to all sets of real numbers if and only if there is an [[atom (measure theory)|atomless]] probability measure on the power set of some non-empty set.

{{harvtxt|Solovay|1971}} showed that existence of measurable cardinals in ZFC, real-valued measurable cardinals in ZFC, and measurable cardinals in ZF, are [[equiconsistency|equiconsistent]].

=== Weak inaccessibility of real-valued measurable cardinals ===

Let <math>\mu</math> be an outer measure on a set <math>X</math>. Say that a cardinal number <math>\alpha</math> is an ''Ulam number'' if whenever<ref>{{harvnb|Federer|1996|loc=Section 2.1.6}}</ref><ref group=nb>The notion in the article [[Ulam number]] is different.</ref>

{{NumBlk|*| <math>\mu(X)\leq\infty</math>,|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
{{NumBlk|*| <math>\mu(\{x\})=0</math> for every <math>x\in X</math>,|{{EquationRef|2}}}}
{{NumBlk|*| all <math>A\subseteq X</math> are [[Carathéodory-measurable set|{{math|''μ''}}-measurable]],|{{EquationRef|3}}}}
then <math>|X|\leq\alpha</math> implies <math>\mu(X)=0</math>.

Equivalently, if <math>F</math> is a set of pairwise disjoint subsets of <math>X</math>, <math>\alpha</math> is an Ulam number if whenever

# <math>\mu(\textstyle\bigcup F)<\infty</math>,
# <math>\mu(A)=0</math> for <math>A\in F</math>,
# <math>\textstyle\bigcup G</math> is <math>\mu</math>-measurable for every <math>G\subset F</math>,
then <math>|F|\leq\alpha</math> implies <math>\mu(\textstyle\bigcup F)=0</math>.

The smallest infinite cardinal [[Aleph-zero|{{math|ℵ<sub>0</sub>}}]] is an Ulam number. The class of Ulam numbers is closed under the [[successor cardinal|cardinal successor]] operation.<ref>{{harvnb|Federer|1996|loc=Second part of theorem in section 2.1.6.}}</ref> If an infinite cardinal <math>\beta</math> has an immediate predecessor <math>\alpha</math> that is an Ulam number, assume <math>\mu</math> satisfies properties ({{EquationNote|1}})–({{EquationNote|3}}) with <math>X=\beta</math>. In the [[Ordinal number#Von Neumann definition of ordinals|von Neumann model]] of ordinals and cardinals, for each <math>x\in\beta</math>, choose an [[injective function]] <math>f_x:x\to\alpha</math> and define the sets

:<math>U(b,a)=\{x\in\beta\mid f_x(b)=a\}</math>.

Since the functions <math>f_x</math> are injective, the sets
:<math>\{U(b,a)\mid b\in\beta\}</math> with <math>a\in\alpha</math> fixed
and
:<math>\{U(b,a)\mid a\in\alpha\}</math> with <math>b\in\beta</math> fixed

are pairwise disjoint. By property ({{EquationNote|1}}) of <math>\mu</math>, the set

:<math>\{b\in\beta\mid \mu(U(b,a))>0\}</math>

is [[countable set|countable]], and hence

:<math>\big|\{(b,a)\in\beta\times\alpha\mid \mu(U(b,a))>0\}\big| \leq \aleph_0\cdot\alpha</math>.

Thus, there is a <math>b_0\in\beta</math> such that

:<math>\mu(U(b_0,a))=0</math> for all <math>a\in\alpha</math>,

which implies, since <math>\alpha</math> is an Ulam number and using the second definition, that

:<math>\mu\Big(\bigcup_{a\in\alpha}U(b_0,a)\Big)=0</math>.

If <math>b_0<x<\beta</math> and <math>f_x(b_0)=a_x</math> then <math>x\in U(b_0,a_x)</math>. Thus

:<math>\beta=b_0\cup\{b_0\}\cup \bigcup_{a\in\alpha} U(b_0,a)</math>.

By property ({{EquationNote|1}}), <math>\mu(\{b_0\})=0</math>, and since <math>|b_0|\leq\alpha</math>, by ({{EquationNote|3}}), ({{EquationNote|1}}) and ({{EquationNote|2}}), <math>\mu(b_0)=0</math>. It follows that <math>\mu(\beta)=0</math>. The conclusion is that <math>\beta</math> is an Ulam number.

There is a similar proof<ref>{{harvnb|Federer|1996|loc=First part of theorem in section 2.1.6.}}</ref> that the supremum of a set <math>S</math> of Ulam numbers with <math>|S|</math> an Ulam number is again a Ulam number. Together with the previous result, this implies that a cardinal that is not an Ulam number is [[inaccessible cardinal|weakly inaccessible]].
